evals.prompt: Review our multiplayer shooter's AWS environment against the Games Industry Lens. Game servers run on Amazon GameLift Spot fleets in us-east-1, eu-west-1 and ap-northeast-1 with FlexMatch matchmaking; the backend is API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB with Amazon Cognito for player accounts; patches are served from S3 through CloudFront. We expect 300k CCU at peak. Give us a graded review and what to fix first.
evals.expected_output: A Games Industry Lens review organized by the lens pillars (Operational excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance efficiency, Cost optimization, Sustainability) that grades the lens best practices by their IDs (GAMEOPS, GAMESEC, GAMEREL, GAMEPERF, GAMECOST, GAMESUS) with PASS/FAIL/N/A verdicts, uses the lens risk levels, frames findings in player-impact terms (login, matchmaking, session continuity), covers games-specific checks such as session-aware scaling with game session protection on Spot fleets, latency-based matchmaking per game mode, authenticated backend requests, content access through CloudFront, cost per player, and ends with a severity-ordered action plan of proposals for human approval. Where live resource data is not available it uses N/A with a reason rather than inventing values.
assertions: Findings are organized by the six Well-Architected pillars and reference lens best practices by ID (for example GAMEREL02-BP01, GAMEPERF07-BP01, GAMESEC03-BP02)
Addresses session-aware scaling / game session protection for the Spot game-server fleets and the risk of Spot interruptions to active matches
Addresses matchmaking: latency thresholds or latency policies and separate matchmaking configurations per game mode
Addresses player identity and backend authentication (Cognito password policy, MFA option, authorizers on API routes) and content access control for the CloudFront/S3 patch delivery
Produces a severity-ordered action plan whose items are proposals for human approval, with no resource changes performed

evals.prompt: Our live-service RPG launches Season 2 in three weeks and marketing projects 4x our current concurrent players. Game servers are on EC2 Auto Scaling groups behind Global Accelerator, player data is in DynamoDB and Aurora, login is through Cognito. Are we ready? Check pre-scaling, quotas, matchmaking, DDoS protection and our deployment plan.
evals.expected_output: A launch-readiness assessment against the Games Industry Lens that checks pre-scaled minimums and capacity reservations against the projected 4x peak (GAMEOPS03-BP05), service quota headroom (EC2 vCPUs, Lambda, Cognito, DynamoDB), DynamoDB warm throughput or provisioned capacity versus peak, instance-type diversification in the Auto Scaling groups (GAMEREL02-BP02), session-aware scale-in protection (GAMEREL02-BP01), load testing at projected peak (GAMEOPS03-BP03), a deployment strategy that keeps players in the game with a rollback plan (GAMEOPS03-BP04), Shield Advanced and WAF on player-facing endpoints (GAMESEC06-BP01), matchmaking monitoring (GAMEPERF07-BP03), status page and on-call readiness, and AWS Countdown for the launch. Items that cannot be completed in three weeks are labeled residual risk with a day-of mitigation. Nothing is scaled or changed by the agent.
assertions: Checks pre-scaling of minimum capacity ahead of the launch rather than relying on reactive autoscaling alone, and mentions capacity reservations or raising minimums
Checks service quota headroom against the projected peak
Checks that scale-in or deployments will not terminate instances hosting active player sessions
Checks DDoS protection (AWS Shield Advanced) and WAF on the player-facing endpoints or accelerator
Frames items against the three-week timeline, labeling anything that cannot be completed in time as residual risk with a mitigation
Does not perform or claim to perform any scaling, quota or deployment change

evals.prompt: Audit our GameLift FlexMatch matchmaking setup: rule sets, latency policies, queue destinations and the alarms we have on player wait time. Players in South America complain about long queues.
evals.expected_output: A focused assessment of the matchmaking area (GAMEPERF07-BP01, GAMEPERF07-BP02, GAMEPERF07-BP03, GAMEOPS03-BP05) that reviews FlexMatch rule sets and whether each game mode has its own matchmaking configuration, queue destinations and player latency policies and whether they exclude the Regions with capacity, FlexMatch and queue CloudWatch metrics (TimeToMatch, TicketsTimedOut, PlacementsFailed, FirstChoiceOutOfCapacity, AverageWaitTime) and alarms on them, and whether there is a hosting location near South American players. It explains the long queues as a hypothesis backed by the metrics to check (not enough players in the mode/Region for the rules, latency policy exclusion, no nearby capacity) and offers the full lens review as a follow-up.
assertions: Reviews FlexMatch rule sets and whether matchmaking configurations are separated per game mode
Reviews queue player latency policies and destinations, including whether latency rules could exclude Regions that have capacity
Names matchmaking or queue CloudWatch metrics such as TimeToMatch, TicketsTimedOut, PlacementsFailed, FirstChoiceOutOfCapacity or AverageWaitTime and whether alarms exist on them
Considers hosting-location proximity for South American players as a cause of long wait times
Answers the narrow question first and offers the full Games Industry Lens review rather than running every check

evals.prompt: Run only the Security pillar of the Games Industry Lens on our studio's production account. Players log in with Cognito, downloadable content is on S3 behind CloudFront, and we have had account-hijacking complaints.
evals.expected_output: A Security-pillar review that grades the GAMESEC best practices (security foundations, ongoing security, player identity and access management, content access control, detection, infrastructure protection, incident response for bad actors, application security, automate security, threat modeling) with PASS/FAIL/N/A and lens risk levels, prioritizes the account-takeover path (Cognito password policy, MFA option, threat protection, WAF bot control), checks that S3 content is reachable only through CloudFront with signed access for private content, and marks the other pillars as out of requested scope rather than grading them.
assertions: Grades Security-pillar best practices by GAMESEC IDs and does not present findings for the other pillars as graded (they are marked out of scope or N/A)
Addresses the account-hijacking complaint through player password policy, optional MFA and account-takeover or bot protections
Checks that downloadable content on S3 is not public and is served through CloudFront with origin access control and signed URLs or cookies where private
Includes detection and response for bad actors (threat detection tooling, a ban or suspension workflow)

evals.prompt: Alarm: GameSessionInterruptions and ServerProcessAbnormalTerminations spiked on the ranked-mode GameLift fleet in eu-west-1 at 19:40 UTC. Players report being kicked from matches. The fleet uses Spot instances and a scale-in policy on PercentAvailableGameSessions. Find the root cause.
evals.expected_output: An investigation that first frames impact in player terms (sessions interrupted, players affected, game Region, duration), checks AWS Health for eu-west-1 and the change timeline (fleet, runtime configuration, scaling-policy or build changes), then works the disconnect symptom map: Spot interruptions (InstanceInterruptions, Spot interruption notices), scale-in without game session protection (NewGameSessionProtectionPolicy), server process crashes tied to a build, EC2 network allowance metrics, DDoS, and regional network events. It distinguishes AWS impairment from the studio's own change and from demand or external causes, states the root cause only when the evidence chain is complete, and recommends prevention citing the lens (GAMEREL03-BP01, GAMEREL02-BP01, GAMECOST02-BP03) as proposals, for example moving ranked sessions off Spot or enabling full game session protection.
assertions: States the impact in player terms (interrupted sessions, affected players or CCU, game Region, duration) before infrastructure metrics
Evaluates Spot instance interruptions as a candidate cause, referencing GameLift interruption metrics or EC2 Spot interruption notices
Evaluates scale-in or deployment terminating instances with active sessions, referencing the fleet's game session protection policy
Evaluates game server process crashes and considers a recent build or runtime configuration change
Separates an AWS-side impairment (AWS Health) from the studio's own change and from external causes
Prevention recommendations cite Games Industry Lens best practices and are proposals, with no change performed

evals.prompt: Since our new content drop went live at 17:00 UTC, players cannot log in. API Gateway shows elevated 429 and 5xx on /login, Lambda throttles are climbing, and the DynamoDB players table shows write throttling. Cognito user pool sign-ins are failing intermittently. What is the root cause?
evals.expected_output: An investigation that frames the impact (logins per minute failing, CCU, duration), recognizes the content drop as the demand event, checks AWS Health, then works the login-storm symptom map: Cognito sign-in throttles against its request-rate quotas, Lambda concurrency limits on the login function and provisioned concurrency, API Gateway stage throttling, DynamoDB capacity mode, warm throughput and hot partitions on the players table, and rules out a credential-stuffing attack via WAF and Cognito threat protection signals. It identifies the capacity shortfall(s) in the login path as the cause, attributes them to the content drop demand without pre-scaling, and recommends prevention citing GAMEOPS03-BP05 (pre-scale for peak), GAMEOPS03-BP03 (load test), and GAMEPERF06-BP02 (data store fit), as proposals.
assertions: Identifies the content drop as the demand event correlated with the start of the failures
Evaluates Cognito sign-in throttling against its quotas, Lambda concurrency throttling and API Gateway throttling as candidate causes in the login path
Evaluates DynamoDB write throttling in terms of capacity mode, warm throughput or provisioned capacity and possible hot partitions
Considers and addresses the possibility of a bot or credential-stuffing attack as an alternative explanation
Recommends pre-scaling the login path ahead of events, citing the relevant Games Industry Lens best practice, as a proposal rather than a change

evals.prompt: Matchmaking wait times jumped from 20 seconds to over 4 minutes for our battle-royale mode in us-west-2 starting 02:10 UTC. FlexMatch TicketsTimedOut is up, queue PlacementsFailed and FirstChoiceOutOfCapacity are elevated, and the fleet is at MaxSize. Investigate.
evals.expected_output: An investigation that frames the player impact (wait time, timed-out tickets, affected mode and Region), checks AWS Health and recent changes to rule sets, queues, fleet capacity or scaling policies, then determines that session placement is failing for lack of game-server capacity: fleet at MaxSize, fleet events for scaling failures or InsufficientInstanceCapacity, Spot pool exhaustion, EC2 vCPU or GameLift quotas, and whether queue latency policies exclude other locations that have capacity. It distinguishes a demand surge from a change or an AWS impairment, names the capacity ceiling as the root cause when the evidence supports it, and recommends prevention citing GAMEOPS03-BP05 (pre-scale), GAMEREL02-BP02 (multiple instance types), and GAMEPERF07-BP01 (latency thresholds), as proposals.
assertions: Frames the impact in player terms (matchmaking wait time, timed-out tickets, affected game mode and Region)
Connects FirstChoiceOutOfCapacity / PlacementsFailed to game-server capacity: fleet MaxSize reached, scaling failures, insufficient instance capacity or Spot exhaustion, or quota limits
Checks whether queue player latency policies or rule-set changes exclude locations that still have capacity
Separates a demand surge from a studio change and from an AWS-side event before naming the root cause
Cites Games Industry Lens best practices for prevention (pre-scaling, instance diversification, latency thresholds) as proposals

evals.prompt: Our game writes the leaderboard and player stats synchronously when a match ends and the match-end screen hangs under load. What does the Games Industry Lens say we should do?
evals.expected_output: A direct answer grounded in the lens: move non-latency-sensitive work such as leaderboard and stats updates to asynchronous workflows (GAMEPERF05-BP02) using queues like Amazon SQS, let the client fetch results afterward, and loosely couple non-critical features so their failure does not block gameplay (GAMEREL03-BP02) with timeouts, retries and backoff and graceful degradation in the client. It explains the player benefit and offers to review the relevant checks against the account.
assertions: Recommends moving leaderboard and stats writes to an asynchronous workflow (for example a queue such as Amazon SQS) with the client fetching results later
Cites the relevant Games Industry Lens best practices (GAMEPERF05-BP02 and GAMEREL03-BP02 or their titles)
Explains loose coupling and graceful degradation so a leaderboard failure does not block the match-end flow

evals.prompt: We are streaming a live football final to 5 million concurrent viewers next month on our OTT platform with CloudFront and MediaPackage. Are we ready for the event?
Run a Well-Architected review of our insurance claims processing application on EKS and Aurora.
